verdicts.flaw_description: Two of the four runs have measurement dates that precede the switch: run One 'switched 4 May' but 'ran 6 minutes shorter by 29 March', and run Three 'switched 5 October' but measured 'by 30 September'. Those savings were recorded before the coolant was in use, so they cannot be its effect (compounded by the insert-grade control covering only 'its machines' while 'every logged run was cut on a machine hired from outside').

A named alternative cause reaches all four sections: 'The central syllabus set coursework at a third of the final grade, up from a quarter, and every section was marked to that central syllabus.' Raising coursework's weight from 25 to 33 percent of the final grade would by itself raise coursework completion, so the 6-to-11-point gains cannot be attributed to the lab kit.

The measured population is narrower than the claim: 'Figures cover the orders rung up at the new prices, and about a fifth of each line's orders were rung up at the old prices.' Roughly 20 percent of each line's post-change orders are excluded from the revenue-per-order figures, so the 4-to-7 percent gains describe a selected subset of orders rather than the line's revenue per order.

The absence figures cover a narrower group than the cohort the claim is about: they 'cover the pupils on the revised timetable throughout', yet 'about a fifth of each cohort spent weeks on the old timetable' and is therefore excluded. The 4-to-7 percent drop is measured on the fully-compliant four-fifths, not on the cohort.
